Question: How did you handle failure?
Old_Answer: As we all know, failure is never fun. But keep in mind that how I deal with it really depends on the specific situation. In some cases, I’d just move on. Most failure are not catastrophic, after all. When I was younger, and single, if I asked a girl out and she said “no” than I’d move on and ask someone else. I take the same position at work. If I proposed an idea, and its rejected, I just move on to something else. There are plenty of ideas that will follow. In other words, I don't hang all of my self-esteem on just one event. Now, if the failure is a project, as in the prototype did work, then it became a chance to learn. To do a deep dive and analyze why it failed. And again, a failure or setback of this nature does not derail the entire project. Infact, you want to be agile: fail fast! Then learn all you can't and try again, applying all of the lessons learned. To quote Hannibal Smith: The Opera is not over until the fat lady sings! To expand on this idea here, is don't quit too early. Some people are good at snatching defeat out of the jaws of victory. I’m not one of them. Now, in some cases there is the “sunk cost” fallacy in which you keep pouring time & money into a doomed project. There are times to give up. If that's the case, I just move on. But again, sometimes you learn the most from such failures, so keep that in mind. You can't unlearn something. The IBM “stretch” computer in the early 60’s was a commercial failure, but 80% of its design was used in the System 360 (which is considered one of the most successful products of all time). So, i believe that a single failure is not the end of the world! It can set you up for something better, if you have the right mindset.

Question: What are the advantages of studying engineering technology over traditional engineering?
Old_Answer: Engineering technology’s only real advantage is that being algebra-based is “easier’ that full-out engineering. It is also more hand-on, if that's your interest. Now, I have seen people with engineering technology degrees get hired as full-blown engineers, even in companies like Johnson & Johnson. One of my former coworkers had one from ODU, he now is the Director of Operations in the company he now works for. However, the federal government will only hire engineering with ABET accredited degrees. So, no NASA job! On the other hand, most states will allow you to earn a PE with a technology degree, but just one example, in Virginia you need twice the experience. Personally, a full-on engineering degree is a safer bet, all things being equal. But if that is not an option, a technology degree will still allow you to work in a technology field.

Question: What contributed to the rise of the personal computer?
Old_Answer: Several things were needed for the “rise” of personal computers. The invention of the microprocessor was vital, and probably goes without saying. The advent of relatively low-cost microprocessors made “home computers” possible. Closely related were low-cost memory chips. And while I like more conventional static RAM, it was dynamic RAM that made memory cheap. Nevertheless, early computers had very limited amounts of memory. In the early 80, it was not uncommon for a computer to have 16k of RAM, with upgrades available for (way) more money. That was one reason why the commodore 64 was such a big hit. The biggest problem between early computers was lack of compatibility. Each manufacturer had their own OS, and even worse, often different formats for floppy disks. So, you could not, for example, work on a document at home on your C64 and take it to work and read the disk on an IBM PC. Because of this, I bought my first MS-DOS machine in 1989 ($1200 for a single floppy “Laser Compact XT” with 512k of ram. I later upgraded it to 640k and figured out how to make a floppy extension cable so I would have a B drive! Keep in mind that MS-DOS and the IBM architecture created a “safe, conservative” environment for business users. The development of VisiCalc and work processers (WordStar) make the PC important to the office at work. There was even a early PC-version of AutoCAD (one of my professors even said he got a math coprocessor, which was also a thing). People don't think about this much, but the lowly dot matrix printer also was an important factor in the adoption of PC’s. It enabled the PC to replace the typewriter in the office, but also make computers useful for students (using word processors to write papers). I was one of them who went through that transition from typing papers to writing them using a word process (I used “Easy Writer” because it was cheap! It really was a game changer! The irony is many printers used the standard Centronics interface, or the RS-232 serial port. It was displaced in the late 90’s and early 2000s by USB, but unlike the floppy issue, there were fewer compatibility issues. I already alluded to software like WordStar and VisiCalc, but one can't overlook the fact that having commercial software that made a computer actually useful for most users was also vital to adopting a personal computer. Most people objection back them was “what am I going to use a computer for” and such software . The irony is very few people used then for storing recipes or creating “databases” for their stamp collection. Games were also a contributor, but dedicated game machine did the job better for many years. And while modems allowed users to connect to BBS systems, the world wide web is probably the tipping point for universal adoption. Web applications like shopping gave most people a reason to have a computer, hence the faster adoption rates in the late 90’s. It also gave rise to instant messaging & social media. Hence, you reading this answer. Been there, done that!
Answer_with_writing_sample: The rise of the personal computer can be chalked up to a perfect storm of factors. First off, technology had to catch up—think about it, back in the day, computers were these giant, clunky machines that took up whole rooms! But then, with the advent of microprocessors in the 70s, you got a more compact and affordable option popping up. Next came software; user-friendly operating systems, like Apple’s Lisa and later Windows, made it easier for everyday folks to hop on the tech train without needing a degree in computer science. Also, let’s not forget the economic boom of the 80s—people had more disposable income and were itching to get a piece of that tech action. Plus, the cultural shift towards personal computing—remember those ads touting “a computer on every desk”? They weren't kidding! Altogether, those elements converged to transform computers from corporate tools into household staples, paving the way for the tech-savvy world we live in today!
Answer_with_user_profile: The rise of the personal computer (PC) in the late 20th century can be attributed to a convergence of technological advances, market demand, and cultural shifts. Firstly, the miniaturization of components, particularly transistors and integrated circuits, made computers more affordable and accessible. Innovations like the microprocessor in the early 1970s enabled manufacturers to create compact and powerful machines suitable for individual users. Additionally, the development of user-friendly operating systems, such as MS-DOS and later Windows, made computers more approachable for non-technical users, further expanding the potential market. The emergence of software applications tailored to personal and business use fueled demand, leading to a burgeoning ecosystem where users could find programs for everything from word processing to gaming. The cultural zeitgeist of the 1980s and 1990s, characterized by a growing interest in technology and an emphasis on personal empowerment, also played a critical role. The marketing strategies employed by companies like Apple and IBM helped frame computers as essential tools for personal productivity and creativity, appealing to a broad audience beyond just tech enthusiasts. Furthermore, the increasing availability of educational resources about computing helped demystify the technology, encouraging adoption. Finally, the affordability of PCs driven by competition among manufacturers opened the floodgates to a wider demographic, allowing individuals, families, and small businesses to harness the power of personal computing, ultimately transforming how we communicate, work, and play in the modern era.
Answer_with_full_information: The rise of the personal computer (PC) in the late 20th century can be attributed to a confluence of technological advancements, market dynamics, and cultural shifts. First and foremost, the development of microprocessor technology in the early 1970s, spearheaded by companies like Intel and AMD, drastically reduced the size and cost of computing components. This made it feasible to design computers that were compact and affordable enough for individual consumers and small businesses. Alongside hardware innovation, the proliferation of software, particularly user-friendly operating systems like MS-DOS and later Windows, empowered users who lacked technical expertise to navigate computers with ease. Moreover, the home computing boom of the 1980s and early 1990s coincided with an expanding internet, which transformed PCs into portals to a wealth of information and networking capabilities. Access to affordable hardware and software, increasing consumer demand for personal computing, and the cultural embrace of technology culminated in a significant rise of personal computers, reshaping how we work, communicate, and entertain ourselves.

Answer_with_writing_sample: Absolutely, you can mix and match speakers and amplifiers, but there are a few key points to consider. Think of it like matching your favorite pair of shoes with just the right outfit; some combinations work beautifully, while others can lead to disappointment. First off, pay attention to the impedance ratings—most home audio gear is designed for either 4, 6, or 8 ohms. If your amp can handle a lower impedance than your speakers, you’re usually good to go. However, connect speakers with too low of an impedance, and your amp might overheat. Next, consider the power handling; your speakers should be able to handle the output of your amplifier without blowing a fuse—or worse, a cone! Lastly, while sound performance can differ wildly based on synergy, don’t let that deter you from experimenting. Old_Answer: Depends. If it is a physical switch, like on the wall of your bedroom? Then no, you have physically disconnected the device from a source of power as effectively as unplugging it. But most devices now have a electronic switch, and your power supply is still working, though in standby mode. Some devices that had transformer-based power supplies switch the DC output vs the line voltage (I saw that on several “boom boxes”) Nevertheless, in both cases you have a phantom current draw. I figured it would supply my phantom power usage. I later add 2 more 300-watt panels, then then added six more 400-watt panels, this time by professionals.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Yes, you are technically charged for electricity if the switch is on and the plug is connected, even if the appliance is not in use, but let’s break it down a bit. Think of it like this: when an appliance is plugged in and the power is on, it’s like a car in the driveway with the engine running—it's not going anywhere, but it's still consuming fuel, or in this case, electricity. Some appliances, especially older ones, let out a little "vampire power" or standby power, meaning they use a small amount of energy just by being plugged in. However, if the appliance is completely turned off and not in standby mode, the energy consumption is likely negligible, although you're still technically "on" the grid. So, if you’re trying to save a few bucks, consider unplugging those culprits when you’re not using them—it’s a simple way to reduce that bill!
Answer_with_user_profile: Yes, you are typically charged for electricity if the switch is on, the plug is connected, but the appliance is not in use, depending on the type of appliance. This phenomenon is often referred to as "phantom load" or "vampire power." Even when an appliance is turned off, many devices still draw a small amount of electricity when they are plugged in—this is known as standby power. Common culprits include televisions, chargers, microwaves, and gaming consoles, which can continue to consume energy even in a so-called "off" state. To mitigate these costs, consider using power strips that can be easily switched off when the devices are not in use, or unplugging appliances altogether. While the amount of electricity consumed in standby mode may be relatively minor, it can accumulate over time, potentially resulting in higher electricity bills. In some households, standby power can account for 5% to 10% of total energy consumption. Therefore, it's a good practice to be aware of which devices remain plugged in and powered, even if they appear to be off. By effectively managing your appliances, you can save energy and reduce unnecessary costs on your electric bill.
Answer_with_full_information: Yes, you can still be charged for electricity even if the switch is on, the plug is connected, but the appliance is not actively being used. This scenario typically applies to what we call "phantom loads" or "vampire energy." Many modern appliances and electronic devices continue to draw a small amount of energy when they're plugged in, even if they are turned off. This is often because they have features like standby modes, remote controls, or timers that allow them to maintain a minimal level of functionality. Over time, these small charges can add up and inflate your electricity bill. For instance, devices like chargers, televisions, and gaming consoles are notorious for this. To mitigate this extra cost, consider unplugging appliances when they are not in use or investing in smart power strips that cut off power to devices when they are not actively being used. Additionally, becoming aware of your energy consumption habits can lead to more efficient energy use, which is not only beneficial for your wallet but also for the environment. So, although it may seem like you're not using electricity, your devices can still contribute to your overall consumption, and those charges can appear on your bill.

Question: If you could be 18 all over again, would you still choose to go to college?
Old_Answer: Of course. But keep in mind that I am the poster child for a non-conventional student earning a degree. My entire education was earned going to school part-time (night school) while being enlisted in the USAF. In fact, I enlisted in the Air Force because they had their own community college (CCAF) so I knew they took off-duty education seriously. That said, I work as an engineer. I could not of had that specific career without my degree. And note that I wrote these answers… The theme of the above answer is that I have really enjoyed my career. I was able to travel some and was able to work on various cool projects. Maybe not as cool as working for NASA or even Google, but I still have done well for myself. By the way, this is my #1 answer by a large margin! Now, had I enlisted and only received the technical training they provided, and never took another class in my life, I could have still been hired for the technician job with the Virginia State Police Communications Division.
